title: Fauquier Housing Needs Assessment
text:
About this study
This technical report presents a comprehensive housing needs assessment for Fauquier County, Virginia, including the Town of Warrenton and Bealeton Census Designated Place (CDP). The study was commissioned by Fauquier Habitat for Humanity (FHFH) with funding from the PATH Foundation and produced by HDAdvisors.
The assessment covers:

Current housing inventory and recent production trends
Demographic shifts and socioeconomic factors shaping housing demand
Ownership and rental market dynamics
Affordability gaps by income level, tenure, and household type
Vulnerable and special-needs populations
Projected future housing needs through 2050

A distinguishing feature of this study is its sub-county focus: where data permit, findings are disaggregated to the Town of Warrenton and Bealeton CDP — the county’s two main population centers — to support targeted policy and program decisions.
Interviews were conducted to understand the reality that community members face on the ground in Fauquier County. Six interviews were completed with nine community members representing employment (2), local government (2), development (1), and real estate sectors (1).

title: Executive summary
text:
Key findings
Fauquier County has a highly priced housing market with a moderate working income environment, where the majority of residents commute away for work and those working within the county must commute in. The county is housing affluent households that commute elsewhere for high paying work, but it sustains short term and lower wage employment where workers must live elsewhere.
Findings below draw on the data chapters. They are also informed by six interviews with nine people from employment, local government, development and real estate. Their perspectives appear in the “What we heard” notes.

title: Executive summary
text:
Supply and structure
Housing choices are very limited. Single-family detached homes are 85.1% of Fauquier’s housing stock, compared with 61.3% in Virginia. The 266 permits per year issued over 2020–2025 were almost entirely single-family, including a jump to 417 in 2025, and 2–4 unit “missing middle” production is effectively zero across the full 2000–2025 record. Rentals are mostly houses, and the subsidized stock is thin and aging. Single-family homes make up about 68% of renter-occupied units and purpose-built apartments about 20%. The county’s entire assisted inventory is 874 units across 13 properties, and 8 of those have a subsidy expiring by 2036. Rental Market →

Affordability
Fauquier is a bedroom community with a lower-wage local job base. 76.4% of employed residents (26,762 of 35,028) commute out of the county, and the average local job pays $68,000. The county median household income of $130,189 is built on wages earned elsewhere. Demographics & Socioeconomics →

The entry-level for-sale market has disappeared. The median sale price reached $650,000 in 2025, and just 6 of 267 active for-sale listings were priced under $350,000. Monthly payments on the median home rose 152% since 2016, against 81% price growth and 43% income growth. Ownership Market →

Housing cost burden is concentrated at lower incomes. 40% of renters are cost-burdened, versus 21% of owners. Every AMI band runs a rental deficit, for a net shortfall of about 3,315 units, and only 22 of 267 for-sale listings are affordable below 100% AMI. NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees identified resistance to growth as a barrier to both housing and employment opportunities across the county. They described a disproportionate burden on the tax base, through rising property taxes and delayed infrastructure costs, that deepens housing affordability challenges.




Need and capacity
Production keeps pace with growth but not with need. The county is projected to add 6,795 households by 2050, requiring about 269 units per year, which is essentially level with the 2020–2025 pace of 266 per year. Adding today’s affordability backlog and replacement of aging stock lifts full-scope need to 12,455 units. Projected Needs →

Figure 7.5
Meeting that need is not possible under current zoning. Remaining by-right capacity inside the eight service districts is plausibly 4,000–4,500 units today, down from the 2010 Comprehensive Plan’s baseline of 8,381 units, after about 4,300 units permitted countywide since 2010. That is below even the roughly 7,000-unit headline need. The county must choose among expanding service districts, increasing density, accepting unmet need, or absorbing rural spillover. Interviewees highlighted the challenge of building housing in Fauquier given limited developable land and service districts, set against the large proportion of land held in conservation easements.

title: 1  Current Inventory and Production Trends
text:
1.1 Study area
Fauquier County is a large, predominantly rural jurisdiction between the Piedmont and the outer Washington, D.C. suburbs with roughly 648 square miles. This study zooms in on the county’s two population centers: the Town of Warrenton, the county seat with about 10,200 residents (2025), and to the south along US-17, the unincorporated Bealeton Census Designated Place (CDP) (~5,000).
Figure 1.1: Two small places anchor a large rural county
Fauquier’s Comprehensive Plan, adopted in 2019, channels growth into eight service districts, where there is public water and sewer service. Conversely, 90% of the county’s land is rural and lies outside these designated service districts, making it largely unavailable for dense development. Furthermore, “…Approximately 107,000 acres or over 25% of the county’s land area is currently in some form of conservation easement or land protection program.”1 Conservation easements alone hold about 57,500 acres of land within Fauquier.2
As a result, housing and development opportunities are concentrated in limited areas of opportunity, near major transportation corridors.3 Bealeton’s service district is located in the southern part of the county, while Warrenton’s covers the center of the county. Marshall Service District covers the north end of the county, nearer to major thoroughfare Route 28. These county service districts are all surrounded by rural designated land use, as well as town-incorporated and planned service districts, like Remington to the south.
Fauquier’s Comprehensive Plan outlines that Bealeton’s Service District, and certain downtown streets of the Marshall Service District may align with an optional Urban Development Area, which would allow the county to accommodate projected growth through increased densities: at least four units per developable acre for single family, eight units/acre for townhomes, and 12 units/acre for multifamily. It is estimated that about 8,381 units of unbuilt capacity remain within the service districts and 97% of permits issued 2001–2018 were single-family detached, reinforcing the low-density pattern.4

title: 1  Current Inventory and Production Trends
text:
1.2 Housing stock composition
Single-family detached homes represent 85.1% of Fauquier’s housing stock. About 86% of all the housing stock in the Greater Piedmont region, including Rappahannock, Culpeper, Orange, and Madison counties, are also single family detached.5 This unit type in the Greater Piedmont REALTOR’s region, as well as in Fauquier alone, is far above Virginia’s overall share of single family detached homes at 61.3%. The county has proportionally little multifamily units. Five+ unit structures are only about 3% of the stock, versus roughly 18% statewide.
5 Source: Greater Piedmont REALTORS, Greater Piedmont Region Housing Gap Analysis (March 2026)





WarningDefinitions



“Single family detached” is defined as one housing unit on one parcel of land. “Single family attached” can be imagined as a townhome, but is not considered “multifamily housing,” as there is likely a property line division through the house. Multifamily is defined as a residential property with multiple units on one parcel: five or more units. Broadly, structures with two and more units are identified as “Missing Middle” housing, and could include a single family attached home like a townhouse.










Figure 1.2: Fauquier County’s housing is far more single-family than Virginia’s





Warrenton and Bealeton carry more multifamily than the county overall, with a larger share of attached and mid-size multifamily units in Warrenton than in Bealeton. Broken down by their counts rather than rates, this statistic is difficult to verify.






WarningData note: small-place estimates



With smaller places, and therefore lower populations for the ACS to precisely size multifamily and manufactured stock, there are limitations on the data available. Anything with low reliability is suppressed, affecting the reliable counts of multifamily units in Warrenton and Bealeton. Only single-family detached counts are reliable (High) in both towns.

title: 1  Current Inventory and Production Trends
text:
1.3 Age of the housing stock
The county’s housing stock is aging, with an overall median year built of 1987 and 56% of all homes were built before 1990. Owned homes skew newer than this, where 34% of owned homes were built in 2000 or later, reflecting the county’s for-sale subdivision growth.
This is in contrast to the rental housing stock, which skews older with about 32% of renter-occupied homes predating 1960. Comparatively, only 12% of owner-occupied homes were built before 1960.
Warrenton’s median year built matches Fauquier (1987), but Bealeton’s stock is meaningfully newer with a median year built of 1998. This is consistent with Bealeton’s role as a recent growth node along US-17.

title: 1  Current Inventory and Production Trends
text:
1.4 Tenure & Vacancies
Across ACS estimates (2013–2024), Fauquier’s owner-occupied share of units has held in the high 70s to 80%. This is remarkably stable, however, the towns diverge sharply in 2024: Bealeton is nearly 79% owner-occupied, while Warrenton is only about 63% owner-occupied, with the county’s clearest concentration of renters.
Ownership is king in Fauquier County, with a few opportunities for renting in Bealeton and Warrenton. This is a signal for a heavily ownership-based market (Chapter 3).








Figure 1.4: Warrenton’s homeownership rate consistently trails the county and Bealeton





Vacancies throughout Fauquier, Warrenton, and Bealeton point to a very tight housing market. Fauquier’s overall vacancy rate is about 6.6% (1,901 of 28,621 units are vacant).
Most of the county’s vacancies are not available housing though, as 550 units are considered seasonal/recreational - perhaps a short term rental - and another 883 are marked as “other vacant” or held off-market, possibly part-time country housing. Effectively, only about 1.2% of all units are actually available: 174 for rent and 178 for sale, a sign of an extremely tight market.7 This has the potential to push local workers, and renters competing for quality space, to take housing opportunities outside Fauquier.
7 Source: ACS 2020–2024, Table B25004.





NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees described a strong word-of-mouth housing market. Employers and workers compete for the same rentals and sales, alert each other to openings, and take over each other’s leases and home shares. Employers said they struggle to hire workers who can find or afford quality rental housing.

title: 1  Current Inventory and Production Trends
text:
1.5 Residential construction
Despite the perceived need that local workers face for units, over the last 20 years permits have overwhelmingly been for single family units. Permitting has averaged 266 units/year over 2020–2025, and is essentially all single-family. Activity jumped in 2025 to 417 units, about 57% above that average and the most in any year since 2006. In the Greater Piedmont REALTOR’s region, about 38.7% of permits were for Fauquier County, while 50% were in Culpeper and 11.6% combined in Madison and Rappahannock.8
8 Source: Greater Piedmont REALTORS, Greater Piedmont Region Housing Gap Analysis (March 2026)Missing middle housing, structures with two to four units, is virtually nonexistent in the study area. Just 10 total 2–4-unit permits were issued across the entire 2000–2025 period. Multifamily (5+ units) is rare and episodic, notable only in a few years: the peak was 194 units in 2006, and the most recent was 48 in 2018. No 5+ unit permits have been issued since, including 2026 through September.
The CoStar property inventory shows two recent rental projects that the permit categories above do not capture as multifamily. Warrenton Chase (100 units, 2023) in Warrenton is built as single-family-style rentals, and Summit at Bealeton (160 units, market-rate, under construction for 2026) is a new garden-apartment community in Bealeton. Together they would add about 260 rental units to a professionally managed market of roughly 1,000 tracked apartments (Chapter 4).
Permitting has continued at a similar pace in 2026. Through September 2026, the county issued 252 residential permits (all single-family), 5% more than the 241 issued over the same months of 2025. The Town of Warrenton accounted for 65 of them (26%), compared with 5 through September 2025 and 7 in all of 2025. Bealeton is an unincorporated CDP whose permits are issued by the county, so they cannot be separated out.








Figure 1.5: Nearly every home permitted since 2000 has been single-family











NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees said the market lacks diversity: no accessory dwelling units, few townhomes, no studios, almost no starter homes, and very little supporting retail. Development is producing large homes on large lots, and essential workers, aging residents hoping to downsize, and young people hoping to return are not finding options.

title: 1  Current Inventory and Production Trends
text:
1.6 New construction vs. resale
Of note is the difference in median home price for new construction versus resold homes, as well as lot size.
New construction in the County sold for a higher median price in 2025 (~$734,000 vs ~$635,000 for resales) and was larger than resale homes. New construction had a median square footage of roughly 2,854 versus 370 less for resale homes.








Figure 1.6: New homes are larger and pricier than resales but sit on smaller lots





That said, in reality, newly constructed homes sit on far smaller lots, 0.23 versus 1.0 acre for resale. New-construction lot sizes have shrunk sharply since 2022, when the median acreage was near 1.68. As unit production has concentrated in service-district subdivisions, this study assumes that lot sizes have had to decrease.
Product type, more than lot size, signals the missing-middle gap. The county’s new supply is made up of larger detached houses, with little to no starter-scale or small-lot infill product entering the market.






NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees saw the same pattern in what is being built: where development happens, homes are bigger than locals need or can afford. They named a gap in the market for smaller, more manageable units, alongside an abundance of larger ones.

title: 2  Demographic Shifts & Socioeconomic Factors
text:
2.1 Population growth
Fauquier has seen steady population growth over the last 35 years, despite consistent descriptions of the county’s similarities over time. Those that grew up in Fauquier still recognize it as the place where they were raised. Fauquier’s population climbed from 48,741 in 1990 to about 76,500 in 2025, a 57% increase, adding some 27,800 residents over 35 years.
Growth throughout has been steady rather than explosive: after a 2021 jump of about 1,070 residents, the county has added about 600 a year since 2022. Warrenton has held at about 10,200 people since 2022, and Bealeton reached nearly 5,000 by 2024. Both towns together hold about a fifth of the county’s residents, but nearly all recent growth has occurred outside them: of the county’s 3,491 added residents from 2020 to 2025, Warrenton accounts for just 165.
Figure 2.1: Fauquier has grown steadily for three decades
With roughly 600 or more residents gained yearly since 2021 and limited residential development areas, the sensation of housing scarcity is felt by newer and long-term residents alike.

title: 2  Demographic Shifts & Socioeconomic Factors
text:
WarningCaveat: mixed sources and universes



The county line splices decennial 100% counts (April 1: 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020) with Population Estimates Program figures (July 1: 2021–2025); Warrenton’s recent points are also PEP, while Bealeton’s 2024 point is an ACS 5-year estimate. These are different universes and reference dates — small level differences between series are expected, not real change. Bealeton has no 2000 decennial place record and is not published in the PEP, so its line starts in 2010; its apparent dip from the 2020 count to the 2024 ACS estimate likely reflects that change of source rather than population loss. Documented in Appendix A.

title: 2  Demographic Shifts & Socioeconomic Factors
text:
2.2 Components of change
Net migration, people moving in from elsewhere, far outweighs natural change, births within the county compared with deaths, as the county’s growth engine. The county grows chiefly because more people move in (+586) than are born there (+57). Natural increase is thin and shrinking: 722 births barely exceeded 665 deaths, down from a natural gain of 59 the year before, which is consistent with an aging population.








Figure 2.2: Migration drives Fauquier’s growth more than natural increase





Migration is overwhelmingly domestic (+539) with a smaller international component (+47). People relocate to Fauquier from elsewhere in the U.S., largely the D.C. metro.

title: 2  Demographic Shifts & Socioeconomic Factors
text:
2.3 Age structure
As implied by natural population change, Fauquier has a notably thin young-adult band: just 13% of residents are 18–34, versus 16% statewide. Young adults tend to leave and often do not return, a pattern tied to a lack of viable positions and entry-level housing (see Chapter 3 and Figure 2.8).
The county skews toward established working-age adults: 35–64-year-olds are its largest group, feeding demand for family-sized housing. Seniors are a modestly larger and growing share of Fauquier’s population: 17.2% are 65+, edging above Virginia’s 16.7% and rising, as the 35–64 cohort ages in place.








Figure 2.3: Fauquier has fewer young adults than Virginia











NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees said young people who leave Fauquier typically do not return, for lack of viable jobs and entry-level housing. They wondered how to recruit young people to the county while also helping seniors age in place.








TipTown spotlight — two very different age profiles



The towns diverge in age sharply. Warrenton is the county’s oldest community: about 18% are 65 and older (High reliability). Bealeton is markedly younger, with roughly 7–8% seniors and a large under-18 share, reflecting its role as a family-oriented growth node.

title: 2  Demographic Shifts & Socioeconomic Factors
text:
2.4 Households
Married-couple families represent 60% of Fauquier’s households, well above Virginia’s 49%, with an average household size of 2.78, also larger than the state’s 2.52.








Figure 2.4: Warrenton has far more people living alone than the county





Warrenton looks structurally different: people living alone are its single largest household type (41%), and its average household is just 2.49. This profiles Warrenton as a center for small-town rentals that can serve aging seniors.
Bealeton runs the other way: family-heavy (54% married-couple) with the largest average household (3.11), pointing to demand for larger, family-sized homes.






WarningReliability



Town composition shares are Medium reliability (CV 15–30%) for most categories — Bealeton’s “other non-family” slice is Low (CV > 30%) — so read the town bars as broad profiles, not precise shares. Both towns’ average household sizes are High reliability.

title: 2  Demographic Shifts & Socioeconomic Factors
text:
2.5 Household income
At $130,189 annually, Fauquier’s median household income is the third-highest of its peer set, after Prince William and Loudoun. Fauquier is essentially tied with Prince William in median income and is far below fast-growing Loudoun ($181,765).








Figure 2.5: Fauquier’s median income ranks third among its peers





Conversely, Warrenton’s median income, $83,331, is the lowest in the comparison and below the statewide median income of $93,170. Bealeton’s median income of $108,224 lands between the two. High county-wide income coexists with a lower-income Warrenton core, while Bealeton tracks closer to the county: a spatial income gap that shapes where affordability pressure concentrates.






NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees described the county’s wealth as held in its rural areas and concentrated in the northernmost part of the county, closest to the highways that connect commuters to higher wages in D.C.








WarningReliability



Warrenton’s median is High reliability (CV 5%); Bealeton’s is Medium (CV 17%, ±$30,504), so its position relative to the county should be read as approximate.










Figure 2.6: Real incomes have risen only modestly after adjusting for inflation





Nominal median income rose 55% over 2010–2024 from $83,877 → $130,189, but most of that reflects inflation. In constant 2024 dollars, real income only grew about 15% with real buying power creeping up, not surging, even as home prices climbed far faster (see Chapter 3).
Fauquier as a whole is high-income: 44% of households earn $150,000 or more — nearly double Virginia’s share of high earners. Warrenton is the lower-income town: about 27% of its households earn under $50,000 per year versus 17% of households county-wide. Warrenton also has the smallest share of earners in the top ($150k+) bracket.








Figure 2.7: Warrenton households skew lower-income than Bealeton or the county





Bealeton mirrors the county more closely, concentrated in the upper-middle and $150k+ income brackets, consistent with its higher median income.






WarningReliability



Bealeton’s three lowest income brackets carry coefficients of variation above 30% and are suppressed here; the shown Warrenton and Bealeton cells are Medium-to-High reliability.








TipPoverty — county low, town contrast



Fauquier’s overall poverty rate is 6.8% (about 5,000 people), which is below Virginia’s 9.9%. The town rates are less certain and are best read as counts: roughly 950 people live in poverty in Warrenton and 80 in Bealeton, with margins too wide to publish reliable place-level rates (both CV > 30%). The takeaway is directional — poverty is low county-wide and modestly concentrated in Warrenton.1


1 Source: ACS 2020–2024, Table S1701 (S1701_C01_001 universe, S1701_C02_001 count, S1701_C03_001 rate).

title: 2  Demographic Shifts & Socioeconomic Factors
text:
2.6 Employment
The county is a modest job center relative to its neighbors to the north and east: it adds workers steadily, but has not captured the metro’s fastest employment expansion. That said, Fauquier’s at-place employment grew from 21,549 jobs in 2015 to 23,920 in 2025, an increase of about 11%.
This growth roughly matches the statewide pace, but is well behind Loudoun, which saw about a 33% increase in employment, alongside a 19% increase in employment for Prince William for the same time period.








Figure 2.8: Fauquier’s job base has grown but slower than its metro neighbors





Slower job growth reinforces the commute-out pattern — many residents work in higher-growth counties to the east (see Figure 2.10).
Fauquier’s all-jobs average pay was about $68,000 in 2025, which is mid-pack among its peers, with Culpeper at $57,600 and Prince William near $66,000, but far below Loudoun with $87,100.








Figure 2.9: Only Loudoun outpays Fauquier across all jobs





The county’s largest employers by sector are local government (including the school systems), retail, health care, and construction. Most pay modestly: health care averaged $60,100 yearly and retail trade just $41,900, the lowest-paying of the sectors shown in every county; only accommodation and food service pays less locally, at about $28,100. Construction is the exception at about $74,800. Wage growth has kept pace with neighbors, with all four counties seeing all-jobs pay rise 42–48% since 2015 (QCEW trend 2015→2025, not shown in the chart above).
Wage growth has held along neighboring counties. The gap is one of level, not trajectory — Fauquier simply has fewer of the high-wage jobs concentrated to its east and little diversity in its employment sectors.






NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees saw worker opportunity, housing, and economic development as tightly linked. They described an in-county job base that is mostly low-wage, where higher-paying employers have been pushed out by a self-reinforcing cycle: without middle-income jobs, middle-income housing demand stays suppressed, and without that housing, employers struggle to recruit workers who can afford what is available. As one put it, “Fauquier is a bedroom community - people live here and work elsewhere.”








WarningA note on the wage figures



FHFH-computed 2025 QCEW averages run modestly above the Greater Piedmont REALTOR’s study’s earlier $64,272 all-jobs figure (2023 vintage) — the difference is nominal wage growth between vintages, not a discrepancy. Small county-by-sector cells that BLS suppresses for disclosure are excluded, so only complete series (all jobs, health care, local government, retail trade) are shown.



Early 2026: jobs edge up, wages jump
Fauquier added about 170 jobs between 2025 Q1 and 2026 Q1, up 0.7% to roughly 23,800. That outpaces Culpeper and Virginia, where employment was flat, but trails Prince William and Loudoun. The number of private and public establishments did not change.
Average annual wages in Fauquier rose 8.5% over the same period, to $73,060, the fastest increase of any comparison area. Part of this reflects a few sectors. Construction wages rose 13% as the sector added 330 jobs (13%), the largest gain in the county and consistent with the rise in 2026 building permits (Chapter 1). Health care went the other way, shedding about 170 jobs (-6%), the largest loss.

title: 2  Demographic Shifts & Socioeconomic Factors
text:
2.7 Commuting
It’s widely recognized that those who live in Fauquier do not work in Fauquier, impacting the local economy and housing opportunities in both directions. Fully 76.4% of Fauquier’s employed residents commute out of the county: just 8,266 of the county’s 35,028 employed residents work in Fauquier itself. Separately, only 35.4% of jobs located in Fauquier are filled by county residents (8,266 of 23,349 Fauquier jobs), two measures of the same bedroom-community pattern. The largest outbound flows run east into the D.C. job market: nearly 8,200 to Fairfax, 5,400 to Prince William, and 3,000 to Loudoun.








Figure 2.10: Fairfax and Prince William draw the most Fauquier out-commuters





Inbound commuting is the mirror image, but comparatively smaller for Fauquier. The top in-commuter origins are from Culpeper with 2,400 workers incoming daily, followed by Prince William with 2,300, and Fairfax at 1,300, filling local jobs Fauquier residents don’t. The local government officials, teachers, nurses, and gas station attendants are typically driving in.






NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees reiterated that this workforce gap is visible across sectors. More than half of Fauquier Health employees live outside the county, and teachers, firefighters, and government workers face the same commute. Wages suited to the local job base cannot carry local rents or mortgages, and housing suited to local workers is largely nonexistent.


A large share of Fauquier’s working residents, 37%, commute 45 minutes or more daily. This is more than double Virginia’s rate of those who commute that long - 18%. This is a direct consequence of the out-commuting pattern outlined in Figure 2.10.
Long commutes are a regional exurban trait: Culpeper has about 37% of its commuters traveling 45 minutes or more. Prince William looks similar at 36%, while inner-suburb Loudoun has lower rates of long commutes (24%).








Figure 2.11: More than a third of Fauquier commuters travel 45 minutes or more





Within the county, Bealeton commuters travel the farthest, with 39% of commuters traveling 45 minutes or more. Only 31% of Warrenton residents travel that long for work, reflecting Warrenton’s greater share of local, in-town jobs, as well as proximity to transportation.






TipTown contrast: Warrenton and Bealeton



Warrenton and Bealeton are demographically opposite — Warrenton is older, and has more single-person and renter households, paired with lower incomes. Bealeton is younger and family-heavy with higher income (Figure 2.4, Figure 2.7). Affordability pressure and the demographic story both play out differently in the two places.

title: 3  The For-Sale Market
text:
3.1 Sales volume
Figure 3.1: Home sales cooled sharply from the 2020–21 peak
Sales peaked at 1,466 sold in 2021 and have since fallen to 938 in 2025 (down about 36% from the pandemic-era high). The cooling reflects Fauquier’s thin supply and higher financing costs, not falling demand, as prices kept climbing through the slowdown (Figure 3.2).
Counts through 2021 come from the GP/VAR annual series and 2022 onward from Bright MLS; 2026 is a partial year-to-date count (January through October) and is not comparable to the full years. Against the same months of 2025 (798 closings), 2026 volume is roughly flat at 821 (+3%), so the decline has leveled off rather than continued.

title: 3  The For-Sale Market
text:
WarningA note on sales counts



Bright MLS’s published monthly summary reports roughly 20% more sales than the transaction-level export used for the volume series above (e.g. 1,127 vs 938 closings in 2025) — a near-constant level offset across every year, consistent with a property-type filter on the export. Median sale prices agree between the two sources to within ~0.1%, so the price findings are unaffected; the level of sales counts (and the active-listing snapshot below) should be read as the export’s narrower definition, while the year-over-year trend holds under either source.

title: 3  The For-Sale Market
text:
3.2 Prices








Figure 3.2: Prices climbed steeply and kept rising after inflation





The county’s median sold price nearly doubled in nominal terms: about $360k in 2016 to $650k in 2025, an 81% increase. Even after inflation, real prices rose from roughly $465k to $650k in 2025 dollars, a 40% increase in genuine appreciation, not just inflation. So far in 2026 (through October) the county median is $655k.
Homes inside the two towns sell for less than the county as a whole. In 2026 to date, Warrenton’s median runs about $537k and Bealeton’s about $466k, against the county’s $655k; in 2025 the figures were about $576k and $548k. Bealeton’s drop from 2025 to 2026 rests on about 98 sales, so it may reflect the mix of homes sold rather than a real price decline.1
1 Town series begin in 2022 because the county’s 2016–2021 monthly series is VAR (county-only). They come from Bright MLS’s published town-area statistics (annual figures are sales-weighted averages of monthly medians). The ZIP codes that carry the town names cover far more ground: the Warrenton ZIPs (20186/20187) had a 2026 median near $698k and Bealeton’s 22712 near $485k, because they take in large rural parcels well beyond the town limits.

title: 3  The For-Sale Market
text:
3.3 Prices vs. payments vs. incomes








Figure 3.3: Monthly mortgage payments have far outrun both prices and incomes





Over 2016–2025 the median home sales price rose +81%, but the monthly payment on that home rose +152 percent. This is likely a reflection of the 30-year rate that climbed from 2.96% in 2021 to 6.60% in 2025, compounding the price increase. Rates have since climbed further, to 7.33% in October 2026, the highest since November 2023; at that rate the payment on the 2025 median home would be about $4,020 a month, versus $3,730 at the 2025 average. Median household income rose only +43% through 2024, far behind both. Buying power has fallen sharply.2
2 The pattern matches the GP study’s Figure 9 direction (GP: price +79%, payment +127%, income +35%); FHFH’s actuals run somewhat higher on all three but tell the same story — payments ≫ prices ≫ incomes.

title: 3  The For-Sale Market
text:
3.4 Price segments








Figure 3.4: The entry-level segment has all but disappeared





Homes under $250k fell from 3.8% of sales in 2022 to 1.6% in 2025. Everything under $350k is now barely 6% of the market. As of the October 2026 listing snapshot, just 6 of 267 active for-sale listings were priced under $350,000.






NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees identified pricing as the most direct pressure on both housing and business: the county’s stock skews toward high-end ownership, paired with aging but costly rentals. Realtors named starter and downsize homes (often the same unit) as the types missing from the market, and interviewees noted that in April 2026 just three homes were listed under $350,000.


The $750k+ home price band has surged to 35% of sales from 21% in 2022. The modal band is now $500–750k (or 41% of sales).
This is the tail end of a long collapse in the starter home market: the Greater Piedmont REALTOR’s identified that under-$250k sales fell from 27.8% in 2016 to 3.0% in 2021. The MLS-only view here (2022+) shows the effective erosion of the market for entry level homes.






NoteWhat is listed for sale now



As of October 2026, the median asking price across the 267 active for-sale listings is $769,900, well above the $655k median sale so far in 2026. 51% of listings ask more than $750,000, and 1 fall between $250,000 and $350,000. New construction makes up 20% of listings at a median of $905,258. Only 7 listings have two or fewer bedrooms. Bank-owned and corporate-owned listings number just 2, so there is no sign of distressed sales. As with the rental snapshot (Chapter 4), this is a single day’s inventory, so read it as directional.

title: 3  The For-Sale Market
text:
3.5 Days on market & supply








Figure 3.5: Homes still sell fast but with a pronounced seasonal rhythm





Despite the gap in availability of starter-style homes, the housing market (with larger single family homes) is still hot. Homes sell fast with a median 10 to 11 days on the market in 2022 - 2024. This rose to 21 days on the market in 2025, reflecting a cooling effect from increased rates. So far in 2026 (through October) the median is 19 days, little changed from 2025. This is still a matter of weeks, not months.
The monthly view exposes a strong seasonal rhythm that the annual averages can hide. Listings linger on the market for roughly 25 to 40 days in December through February and sell in under 10 days by spring yearly.








Figure 3.6: Inventory has loosened from pandemic lows but supply is still tight





Active for-sale inventory has climbed from a tight 315 listings a month in 2022 to 397 in 2025 and 414 so far in 2026. There’s a real loosening of the pandemic era squeeze with months of supply on the market - 3.4 to 4.4 months, and 4.5 in 2026. The latest published month (October 2026, data through 10/30/2026) shows 324 active listings and 4 months of supply; active listings are 24% below a year earlier (426), so the fall pullback is steeper than last year’s.
Even so, supply stays well below the roughly six-month mark that separates a seller’s from a buyer’s market: Fauquier remains a seller’s market, just a less extreme one than at the 2021–22 peak.
The towns are moving apart. Measured as average listings against average monthly sales, Warrenton holds about 3.3 months of supply in 2026, tighter than the county. Bealeton has loosened the most, from about 2.4 months in 2022 to about 4 in 2026: its active listings roughly doubled, from about 20 to 39, while sales held near 10 a month. Bealeton’s small sales count makes its monthly figures swing widely, so the yearly averages are the better guide.






TipInventory is recovering, not recovered



Contrary to a point-in-time reading, the monthly Bright MLS series shows active listings and months of supply trending upward since 2022 (from ~3.4 months in 2022 to ~4.4 in 2025 and ~4.5 in 2026 to date), though the climb has flattened since 2025, as higher rates slowed the frantic pace. Fauquier is still firmly a seller’s market, with supply short of the ~6-month balance point, and homes selling within weeks for most of the year.

title: 3  The For-Sale Market
text:
3.6 What it takes to buy








Figure 3.7: The median home takes about $75,000 more income than households earn





Homes available for sale in Fauquier are expensive relative to what local incomes can support. That said, both housing prices and incomes have risen in 10 years. However, affording the $650k median home requires about $204,891 in household income under standard underwriting, versus Fauquier’s actual $130,189 median, a gap of roughly $75,000. The gap is driven by the same forces as outlined in Figure 3.3: high prices and a 7.33% mortgage rate. The full owner/renter gap by income band is developed in Chapter 5.
The squeeze is amplified by financing: monthly payments rose far faster than prices or incomes (Figure 3.3).
As new construction skews larger and pricier (Chapter 1), the sub-$350k segment has all but disappeared (Figure 3.4), and the market still moves fast (Figure 3.5). This leaves entry-level buyers with few options at any quality level.






NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees described a quality-versus-price mismatch for buyers: “what’s affordable isn’t desirable, and what’s desirable isn’t affordable.” They said the resulting market works well for high-income commuters but squeezes the county’s own workforce and tax base out of the picture.

title: 4  The Rental Market
text:
4.1 Who rents
Figure 4.1: Warrenton is the county’s clearest concentration of renters
Fauquier is overwhelmingly an ownership county: only about 21% of households rent. For context, 33% of Virginia’s households are renters. Folks come to Fauquier to buy, and there is a limited rental market.
Warrenton is the exception: roughly 37% of the town’s 3,985 households rent, nearly double the county rate. Warrenton represents the county’s principal rental submarket. Bealeton, on the other hand, tracks with the county at about 21% of its households renting.

title: 4  The Rental Market
text:
WarningReliability



Bealeton’s renter count is small and carries Medium reliability, so it is read as a count, not a precise rate.

title: 4  The Rental Market
text:
4.2 What renters pay








Figure 4.2: Every measure of rent has climbed and broker-placed leases run highest





The county’s median gross rent, meaning all housing costs including lease rent and utilities, rose from $1,138 in 2013 to $1,613 in 2024, an increase of 42%. Over the same years, prices for everyday goods and services other than housing rose about 27%, so rents have outpaced general inflation and renters have lost ground.
The other rent measures tell the same story at different price points. CoStar asking rents at the county’s market-rate apartments reached about $1,777 in 2026 Q3, above the ACS median, while the larger set of affordable (rent-restricted or subsidized) apartments asked about $1,529. The MLS median closed lease kept rising after the ACS series ends, from $1,950 in 2022 to $2,500 in 2026 to date; these broker-placed leases skew toward single-family homes and townhouses and price well above the other measures. This report uses the ACS median gross rent as its affordability benchmark (Chapter 5), since it covers the full rental universe, while CoStar tracks only professionally managed apartment communities.






NoteWhat we heard



In spring 2026, an interviewee shared that “Only about 2 of 19 available rentals were priced under $1,700.”


Town rents track the county: Warrenton and Bealeton median 2024 rent (High reliability) sits roughly within $50 to $200 of the county figure.

title: 4  The Rental Market
text:
4.3 Where the rental stock prices








Figure 4.3: Most rentals now price at $1,500 or more





The modal rent band in the county is $1,500–1,999 and represents about 25% of county cash-rent renters. Combined with the bands above it, most renters now pay $1,500 or more. Under $1,000 monthly rentals are scarce, representing only about 14% of the county’s renters, underscoring how little of the stock is affordable to lower-income households.






NoteWhat we heard



Realtors in particular recognized the challenges renters face, noting that the MLS median rent sits at $2,450: “It’s an outrageously expensive market.” Rental quality was a consistent topic as well, with interviewees reporting that quality is rarely reflected in the price.


In 2025, the MLS recorded that only 28 of 203 closed leases were under $1,700, about 14%. That share has shrunk quickly, from 35% of leases in 2022 to 10% in 2026 to date. These data identify a median county lease of $2,450 monthly, consistent with the Greater Piedmont REALTOR’s March 2026 study. This leaves a somewhat larger affordable share than the single snapshot of available rentals suggested, but the story is the same: sub-$1,700 rentals are scarce, and most of the rental market prices well above that (Figure 4.3, Figure 4.2). The MLS median runs well above the county’s ACS median gross rent ($1,613) because MLS only captures leases placed through a broker, which skew toward larger single-family homes and townhouses (the bulk of this study’s rental stock) rather than the smaller apartment units that lease in-house and never reach MLS.






NoteWhat is listed for rent now



As of October 2026, the MLS shows 41 active rental listings with a median asking rent of $2,900, well above the 2025 closed-lease median of $2,450 and the $2,500 median across 195 leases closed so far in 2026 (through October 2026). Only 3 listings (7.3%) ask under $1,700, fewer in share than the 2025 closed leases (14%). Asking rents run above closed leases and this is a small single-day snapshot, so read it as directional rather than as a market-wide rent.








WarningData note: place-level distributions



Place-level distributions are noisy; only the higher-count Warrenton bands survive the reliability screen, and they mirror the county’s upward concentration.

title: 4  The Rental Market
text:
4.4 The professional apartment market








Figure 4.4: Apartment rents keep rising at market-rate and affordable properties





The professional rental market is small. Roughly 41 multifamily properties appear in the broader CoStar inventory, and CoStar tracks quarterly rents at 14 apartment properties with about 998 units. Most of those units, about 808, are at affordable properties that are rent-restricted or subsidized; only about 190 are at market-rate properties.
Asking rents at the market-rate properties averaged about $1,777 in 2026 Q3, up 34% since early 2016. Affordable properties asked about $1,529, up 51%. For comparison, prices for everyday goods and services other than housing rose about 29% from 2016 to 2025, so apartment rents of both kinds have outpaced general inflation.
New supply is on the way. Summit at Bealeton, a 160-unit market-rate community in Bealeton, is under construction with asking rents near $2,326. That would nearly double the market-rate apartment units CoStar tracks, at rents well above the current market-rate average (Chapter 1).








Figure 4.5: Apartment vacancy has edged up at affordable properties





Fauquier’s professional rental market remains tight, though slack has crept in. Vacancy across the tracked apartments averaged about 3.5% over the last four quarters (4.0% in 2026 Q3), up from about 1.2% in 2019–2021. Even so, it has been under 3% in 58% of quarters since 2016. The increase sits at the affordable properties, where vacancy reached about 4.5% (3.8% a year earlier); market-rate vacancy is about 1.6%. Much of it comes from one property: The Aspens Apartments (238 units) reports 9% vacancy and 8.3% concessions in the latest quarter.

title: 4  The Rental Market
text:
4.5 Rental stock by structure type








Figure 4.6: Most of Fauquier’s rental stock is single-family homes rather than apartments





Single-family homes are the backbone of the county’s rental market, about 68% of all renter-occupied units (attached and detached). Single-family detached alone is roughly 57% of the rental market.
Purpose-built apartments (5+ units) are only about 20% of rentals, the mirror image of Figure 4.4’s thin professional market. This could be why so much of the rental supply behaves like the for-sale market: the reliance on scattered single-family rentals means renters compete for the same limited housing stock as buyers.1
1 Place-level structure detail is too small to size reliably, so this is shown county-wide.

title: 4  The Rental Market
section: 4.6 Fair Market Rents vs. actual rents
text:
4.6 Fair Market Rents vs. actual rents








Figure 4.7: Metro Fair Market Rents run well above what Fauquier renters actually pay





Because Fauquier is folded into the high-cost Washington, D.C. metro FMR area, the county’s two bedroom (2BR) FMR at $2,246 sits far above the actual ACS median 2BR rent of $1,437. This is a gap of roughly $800.
Small Area FMRs (SAFMRs) pull the benchmark towards what locals actually experience, described as a high cost and scarce rental environment. SAFMRs still land above the ACS median rent at every bedroom size, with the Warrenton and Bealeton 2BR SAFMR ranges from $1,520 to $2,340, with Bealeton (22712) at the lowest.
The practical implication in the differences in FMR and ACS rents is ultimately favorable for voucher holders, with generous payment standards. However, this means FMRs overstate the going asking rental market and can be a poor gauge of local affordability. The ACS medians (Figure 4.2) are the better yardstick for rooting rents into local reality.






NoteWhat we heard



An interviewee noted that metro-based Fair Market Rents give voucher holders generous payment standards relative to what local rents actually are.

Fauquier’s assisted housing rental stock consists of 874 units across 13 federally supported properties. This is a small cushion against the market rents documented above. title: 5  Affordability Gaps
section: 5.3 Who bears the cost: households by income and tenure
text:
5.3 Who bears the cost: households by income and tenure
The divide of housing tenure, renting vs. owning, is ultimately a division of income. Low-income households skew heavily toward renting. Renters are a large share of all households in both the county’s 30% and below and 30-50% AMI bands. Owners dominate in the above 80% AMI bands across the county, Warrenton, and Bealeton.
Overall, Warrenton carries a higher renter share across every income band, consistent with its role as the county’s principal rental submarket. Bealeton’s cells are small and are read as counts, not precise rates.








Figure 5.1: Renters cluster at the lowest incomes while owners dominate the top bands











WarningData note: CHAS universe



CHAS detail sums to roughly 25,900 occupied households county-wide. This is the denominator behind the burden and gap figures that follow.

title: 5  Affordability Gaps
text:
5.4 Cost burden over time (ACS)






WarningDefinition: cost burden



Cost burden is defined as paying more than 30% of household income towards housing costs. This is an important and widely tracked metric, as it can help identify both reasonable payment benchmarks across income bands and help to identify vulnerabilities in the housing market.


Renters in Fauquier are consistently the more cost burdened group: about 40% of renters were cost-burdened in 2024 versus 21% of owners. This is a gap of nearly 20 points that has held across the decade.
Luckily, burden has edged down recently, not up. Since 2013 renter cost burden has moved from 44% down to 40%, while owner cost burden has moved from 29% to 21% over the same time period. This could reflect income growth and refinancing opportunities during the low-rate decade. That said, these burden levels remain high, especially for renters, and the recent rate environment increases for owners (Chapter 3) points in the opposite direction for overall relief.








Figure 5.2: Cost burden has eased since 2013 but renters remain far more burdened





Both towns run hotter than the county on renter cost-burden: 55% of Warrenton’s renters and almost 59% of Bealeton’s renters are cost burdened. These data sit well above the county line (2024).






TipTown spotlight — Warrenton and Bealeton carry the county’s highest renter burden



Both towns run hotter than the county on renter cost burden versus 40% countywide. Warrenton’s cell is High reliability, while Bealeton’s is Medium (CV 15–30%) and is read as a count-based signal, not a precise rate. As the county’s principal rental submarket (Figure 5.1), Warrenton concentrates both the renters and the burden — the same submarket where the affordable-rental deficit (Figure 5.4) bites hardest.

title: 5  Affordability Gaps
section: 5.5 The core picture: burden is concentrated at the lowest incomes (CHAS)
text:
5.5 The core picture: burden is concentrated at the lowest incomes (CHAS)
Overall, renters are more cost burdened than owners within every income band, and severe burden is especially concentrated among the lowest-income renters: the households with the least disposable income to absorb a rent increase or utility cost change.
Burden collapses onto the bottom of the income ladder. At lower than 30% AMI, the vast majority of both renters and owners are cost-burdened. Most of them are severely cost burdened, meaning these households pay half or more of their income towards housing costs. Conversely, above 80% AMI the cost burden all but disappears for renters.








Figure 5.3: Cost burden is overwhelmingly a low-income problem











WarningData note: CHAS vs. ACS burden



Measured on the CHAS universe, county burden is 33% for renters and 20% for owners, lower than the ACS headline (Figure 5.2) because CHAS uses a different denominator; the two are reconciled in the Data & Methodology appendix (Appendix A).

title: 5  Affordability Gaps
section: 5.6 The rental gap: too few homes for the lowest incomes
text:
5.6 The rental gap: too few homes for the lowest incomes
The deepest shortfall in rentals is among the lowest income bands. The county has about 625 fewer rentals that are affordable and available to renter households with less than 30% AMI. These are the households with essentially no market alternative.








Figure 5.4: The county is short about 625 rentals affordable to its lowest-income renters





All income bands run a deficit of rental units for a net shortfall of roughly 3,315 units across the county. As a result, higher-income renters occupy units that would otherwise be affordable to lower-income households, a competition-down-the-ladder dynamic.
The CHAS data behind this gap date to 2018–2022, but more recent lease activity points the same way. Among leases closed through the MLS, the share renting at or below what a 50% AMI household can afford ($1,869) fell from 48% in 2022 to 23% in 2026 to date (Chapter 4). These broker-placed leases skew toward larger homes, so they overstate typical rents, but the direction of change since the CHAS period is clear.






NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees described renting in Fauquier as a “gamble”: renters need to be quick and involved in the word-of-mouth market to get a decent apartment.


The gap is a supply problem, not a targeting problem: even where units are nominally affordable, they are already occupied with higher income households. This leaves the lowest-income renters with the fewest options.

title: 5  Affordability Gaps
section: 5.7 The ownership gap: almost nothing for sale below 100% AMI
text:
5.7 The ownership gap: almost nothing for sale below 100% AMI
Below the 100% AMI price ceiling, there is almost nothing for sale: just 22 of 267 active listings (October 2026 snapshot), effectively excluding low to moderate-income buyers. For lower income bands, 0, 1, 4, 17 active listings are affordable across the 30%, 50%, 80%, and 100% AMI bands.
The overwhelming majority of listings, 245 of 267, are priced only within reach of the 120% AMI band or above, mirroring the median-price gap in Table 5.2. Owner-household counts far exceed affordable listings in every income band below the highest wealth households, so first-time and lower-income buyers face a market with essentially no entry point.








Figure 5.5: Only 22 of 267 active listings are affordable below 100% AMI











NoteWhat we heard



Realtors interviewed said they cannot take on clients seeking homes at $250,000 or less, because they know these households will not find success in Fauquier. The buyers who do are dual-income, high-earning households.

title: 5  Affordability Gaps
section: 5.8 The bottom line: wages don’t reach the cost of housing
text:
5.8 The bottom line: wages don’t reach the cost of housing
The all-jobs average wage ($67,982 annually) narrowly covers the county’s median rent ($64,520 needed), a margin of about $3,462, or roughly 5%. That headline flips, though, once you look sector by sector: Health Care ($60,062), Local Government ($58,079), and especially Retail Trade ($41,898 yearly) all pay below the $64,520 needed. This could lead to greater cost burden for households working in Retail Trade or even the Local Government, or contribute to in and out migration and daily commuting patterns for local workers.
The data bear out that workers cannot afford to both work and live here, most clearly for buying and for the lower-wage sectors: even a two-earner household of two average local jobs ($135,964) falls well short of the $204,891 needed to buy the median priced home. Ownership, not rental, is where the wage-to-cost gap is structural and unavoidable.








Figure 5.6: The average wage covers rent but no wage path reaches homeownership





The message is ultimately structural and systemic: the county’s wage base and its housing costs have decoupled. Dual-income working households are priced out of the ownership market, while the lowest-wage sectors are priced out of the market entirely - both rentals and ownership opportunities. The wage to housing cost gap is not just a perception. This gap of wages and housing costs has become a defining structural feature of Fauquier’s housing market.






NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees repeatedly emphasized that “Workers cannot afford to both work and live here.” Several interviewees shared that they cannot even afford to live in Fauquier despite working there.

title: 6  Vulnerable Populations
text:
6.1 Older adults: a growing, largely aging-in-place population
Of the county’s 9,173 households with a resident aged 65 or older, about 32% (or 2,922 households) live alone, compared to the 17% of one-person households with younger individuals.
Living alone in later life raises housing vulnerability concerns: there is only a single fixed income to cover rising costs and maintenance, let alone possible medical attention. Additionally, with a fixed income, there often aren’t additional funds available to be able to downsize, especially with the effectively non-existent entry level market.
Figure 6.1: Older adults are nearly twice as likely to live alone
This aging and single population is set to grow throughout the years. By 2050, the Weldon Cooper Center projects that there will be roughly 18,208 residents aged 65 and over, and 9,844 aged 75 and up (Chapter 7). This demographic, both the highest age and need group, is the fastest expanding in Fauquier and has implications for the future of housing.
About 84% of the county’s senior householders own their homes. Aging in place overwhelmingly means aging in an owned single-family house, meaning also taking on the maintenance, rising taxes, and accessibility burdens to be able to stay.
Figure 6.2: Senior households are overwhelmingly homeowners
There is a small senior renter population, as well, and they likely have the fewest options locally. The county’s small apartment market (Chapter 4) offers little dedicated senior product, and the county’s tightest affordable-rental deficit falls towards those with the lowest incomes (Figure 5.4). When considering options to move into a different, more accessible home, the market cannot and has not provided for seniors.
Senior renters carry the heavier cost-burden: about 41% of the county’s aging renter households are cost-burdened versus 26% of elderly owners (CHAS defines “elderly” as 62 or older, slightly broader than the 65+ threshold used elsewhere in this chapter). This is the mirror of the tenure pattern seen county-wide (Figure 5.3). Because seniors are overwhelmingly owners (Figure 6.2), owner burden reaches more households in absolute terms, but the renter rate is higher and concentrated among those least able to move because of their age and incomes.
Figure 6.3: Two in five senior renters are cost-burdened
The towns show the same renter-heavier pattern. Senior renters in both Warrenton and Bealeton are burdened at roughly 60%.1 When paired with living with a disability, smaller and accessible homes continue to represent a huge gap in the housing market.

title: 6  Vulnerable Populations
text:
NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees saw wage and housing gaps for both the county’s young and aging residents: young people cannot return, and seniors cannot age in place effectively. They described the fast-growing senior population as a “silver tsunami” and have already picked up on its implications for housing.











WarningReliability



Warrenton carries a larger senior-renter share than the county, consistent with its role as the principal rental submarket (its renter cell is Medium reliability); Bealeton’s senior counts are too small to report reliably (CV > 30%) and are suppressed.





1 These cells rest on very small CHAS samples, so only the county figures are charted here.

title: 6  Vulnerable Populations
text:
6.2 People with disabilities
About 10% of the county population, or 7,134 county residents, report living with a disability, but the prevalence is highly dependent on age. Disability is minimally experienced among children, then rises sharply among those aged 65 and older. Roughly 40% of residents aged 75 and over report having a disability, the same cohort projected to grow most by 2050 (Figure 7.6).
The overlap of disability, advanced age, and homeownership (Figure 6.2) is a direct hook for home-repair and accessibility-retrofit programs, accommodating and preserving households that own but cannot easily adapt or maintain their homes. Additionally, land use permitting cottage style units, or moderately dense entry level homes, could eventually serve both seniors and young people returning to work in Fauquier.








Figure 6.4: Disability reaches two in five residents age 75 and over





Not only does the county need more homes, it also needs homes that are lower cost, accessible, and smaller than those currently available for rent or on the market. A projected surge of over 18,208 residents over 65 by 2050 means that this current mismatch in supply and availability is ultimately a structural one. What seniors and those with disabilities might downsize into is just not available, keeping those seniors householders that would otherwise move in homes that younger returners cannot compete for.

title: 6  Vulnerable Populations
text:
6.3 Single-parent families and family poverty
Of the county’s 7,957 families with children under 18, about 21% (or 1,709 families) are headed by a single parent. The large majority of these are mothers (1,079 single-mother vs 630 single-father families). Single-parent families depend on one income in a market where even two average local wages fall short of the median home price (Figure 5.6). This leaves them heavily exposed to the county’s affordable-rental deficit and ultimately housing cost burdens.
Female-householder families face a poverty rate of 10%, nearly three times the 3% rate for married-couple families, and roughly double the 5% all-family rate.








Figure 6.5: One in five families with children is headed by a single parent











WarningReliability



Town-level single-parent counts are small and both fall below the reliability threshold (CV > 30%), so the figure is reported county-only.


With roughly 2,450 female-householder families county-wide, this is a sizeable group that combines vulnerabilities of lower to moderate income, single earnership, and (often) children — a high-priority segment for deeply affordable rental and ownership assistance.








Figure 6.6: Female-householder families are far likelier to live in poverty





Family poverty and single parenthood compound the housing-cost pressures documented in Chapter 5: the households with the least income are those competing hardest for the county’s scarcest affordable units. Their incomes are proportionately more tied up, leaving little remaining for the cost of moving, increases in utility costs, or glasses for a child. On top of that, with the scarcest units being those that are both low-cost and accessible, single parent households and impoverished families with children are likely competing with single seniors for housing.

title: 6  Vulnerable Populations
text:
6.4 Homelessness






WarningRead these counts carefully



The two homelessness series measure different geographies and are counts, not rates — small single-night or point-in-time tallies that swing year to year.

The Point-in-Time (PIT) trend covers the full five-county Foothills Housing Network region (Culpeper, Fauquier, Madison, Orange, Rappahannock), not Fauquier alone. Only the 2025 count is broken out by county — Fauquier accounted for 96 of the region’s 191 people (Orange and Rappahannock reported zero).
The VDOE McKinney-Vento series is Fauquier-specific (students in Fauquier County Public Schools who lacked stable housing at some point in the year) and uses a broader federal definition than PIT, so the two are not additive and not directly comparable.



The regional PIT count climbed from 146 people in 2018 to a peak near 280 in 2022, held through 2024. It then fell to 191 in 2025, a single year’s drop that especially on small counts should be read cautiously, rather than as an established trend.








Figure 6.7: Regional homelessness rose through the early 2020s then fell in 2025





In 2025, Fauquier accounted for 96 of the 191 unhoused people region-wide or 50% of the regional homelessness population. This is the largest single-county share, though the county-level split exists only for 2025.
Point-in-time counts only capture people who are unhoused at a given moment, on the street or persistently homeless populations. PIT counts tell us who is out on count nights or morning, so they understate the full spectrum of housing instability. School-based McKinney-Vento data (below) can capture housing instability more broadly than a PIT count, as McKinney-Vento focuses on students who lacked fixed, adequate housing at any point in the year instead of solely those who are outside. McKinney-Vento could count students based on their families doubling up with others, staying in a motel, or sleeping on a neighbor’s couch.
McKinney-Vento numbers fell from 191 in the 2020–21 school year to 92 in 2024–25, roughly halving over five years. The decline tracks the post-pandemic recovery that came with record rental assistance expansion. On counts this small, year-to-year movement is volatile and a single school year should not be over-read.








Figure 6.8: Housing-unstable students in Fauquier schools have fallen by half since 2020–21





The McKinney-Vento count (a full school year, broader definition) and the PIT tally (one night, literally homeless) measure different things and should not be ranked against each other. They are a reminder that most housing instability, especially in rural communities, is doubled-up or precariously housed, and not always literally unsheltered or in the street.

title: 6  Vulnerable Populations
text:
6.5 Housing quality and manufactured housing
Housing quality, especially for rentals, can play a real factor in housing costs. A small but real slice of the stock is physically inadequate: about 125 units lack complete plumbing, 395 lack a complete kitchen, and 402 are overcrowded (more than one occupant per room).
These inadequacies affect households differently, but are certainly more manageable with more income. With the limited supply of available rentals priced below $1,613 a month (the ACS midpoint), it’s likely that a significant number of these physically inadequate rentals have costly leases and utilities.








Figure 6.9: Inadequate housing counts are small but real





These are counts, not rates, representing a fraction of a percent of the county’s 28,621 units, but they map directly onto Habitat’s home-repair and critical-repair mission.






WarningReliability



Town-level counts are too small to report reliably; the county figures are the dependable signal, and inadequate units concentrate in the oldest segments of the stock (Chapter 1).








TipWhy manufactured housing matters



Manufactured homes, or mobile homes, are an unsubsidized, naturally-occurring affordable source of housing. This stock is worth preserving; manufactured homes are also more exposed to age, condition, and (for those on rented lots) land-tenure risk.


There are about 470 manufactured homes in the county, only 1.6% of the county’s housing stock. 84% are owner-occupied, making manufactured housing one of the county’s few remaining sources of lower-cost ownership opportunities.








Figure 6.10: Manufactured homes are few but overwhelmingly owner-occupied











TipTown spotlight — Bealeton’s manufactured housing is undercounted by ACS



Manufactured-home and mobile-home communities are a known feature of the Bealeton–Remington area, but the ACS place-level estimate for Bealeton CDP records zero manufactured units. This is because the area’s largest community, Marsh Run (approximately 350 units), sits just southeast of the CDP boundary on Route 17 (Chapter 1), not because there is no manufactured housing nearby. The dependable figure is therefore the county total of 470 manufactured homes; Bealeton’s actual share is understated in the place-level data and should be treated as a known gap rather than a true absence.

title: 7  Projected Housing Needs
text:
7.1 How many more people: population to 2050
Fauquier is undoubtedly growing, even when its growth has been stable since 2000. Fauquier’s population is projected to grow from 74,577 residents in 20241 to 93,171 by 2050, an increase of about 18,594 residents. This 24.9% increase in population drives every downstream housing-need estimate in this chapter.
Figure 7.1: Fauquier is projected to reach about 93,000 residents by 2050
Growth is steady across each decade, from 77,588 in 2030 to 93,171 in 2050. This is a 20.1% gain over twenty years, outpacing Virginia’s projected 14.2% statewide growth until 2050. Warrenton is projected to grow in parallel, from 10,693 residents in 2030 to 12,841 in 2050: up 2,148 residents (also a 20.1% increase).
The latest Census estimates suggest the near-term projection may be conservative. The county reached 76,503 residents in 2025 and has added about 610 a year since 2022. Reaching Weldon Cooper’s 77,588 for 2030 would take only about 220 a year from here. If recent growth continues, the county would pass the 2030 projection early, and the near-term need through 2030 (Figure 7.3) would run higher than shown. Warrenton, by contrast, has held near 10,200 residents since 2022, so its projected growth depends on new housing in the town.

title: 7  Projected Housing Needs
text:
1 The base population is the ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimate, which runs modestly below the PEP July-2025 point-in-time estimate (~76,503) used in Chapter 2; see Appendix A for the reconciliation.








WarningData note: Bealeton



Bealeton has no separate Weldon Cooper projection and is carried through the county totals.

title: 7  Projected Housing Needs
text:
7.2 How many more households
Using the average-household-size method, or the number of occupied housing units multiplied by the average household size, the county grows from 26,720 households in 2024 to 33,515 by 2050. This is about 6,795 net new households or a 25.4% increase in households.








Figure 7.2: The county is projected to add roughly 6,800 households by 2050





Compared with constant-headship sensitivity, which measures projected population outcomes based on the proportion of people in a given demographic group that are a head of household, average household size nearly coincides with an estimate of 33,382 households by 2050 (or 6,662 additional households). Only using headship could over or under estimate the projected growth, because of an increase in young adult headship or conversely more multigenerational families.






WarningData note: choice of method



This is a difference of only about 133 households, so the choice of method does not materially change the total. This 6,795 increased figure is the denominator for the production need (Figure 7.3) and the tenure-by-income allocation (Table 7.1) that follow.

title: 7  Projected Housing Needs
text:
7.3 Can production keep pace?
Based on these estimates, the county needs about 269 new units per year to house the projected growth by 2050, including a 3% vacancy allowance. On the numbers alone, the county’s recent production roughly keeps pace with projected need, essentially level with the 266 units per year the county permitted over 2020–2025. Permitting jumped to 417 units in 2025, well above both, and 2026 through September brought 252 more (241 over the same months of 2025). Every one of those units was single-family, which is why the count alone does not settle whether the county is meeting its need.
The baseline need is lighter in upcoming years, with only about 204 units/year required through 2030, rising toward the recent pace as growth compounds. The build pressure, or need to add units, is in near-term and more specific to the type and price of what is built, not the overall raw count.
This inverts the Greater Piedmont REALTOR’s study’s finding that units needed (307/yr) exceeds the current building pace. The difference in calculations is relative to the household-size assumptions made. This study uses the county’s actual 2020–2024 ACS average household size of 2.78, whereas the GP study’s +7,737-household figure back-implies a roughly 2.7-person household.






WarningWhy household size matters



A larger average person size spreads the same population over fewer new households, ultimately lowering the annual unit need; the full reconciliation is documented in the Data & Methodology appendix (Appendix A).










Figure 7.3: Recent building has roughly kept pace with projected household growth





Keeping pace with the baseline count is admirable but not the same as meeting need, though. The affordability gaps (Figure 5.4, Figure 5.5) show the recent product mix has skewed towards the top of the market. The forward challenge is in composition that can meet the diverse needs of those described in Table 7.1.

title: 7  Projected Housing Needs
section: 7.4 How much does the answer swing? One assumption sets the range
text:
7.4 How much does the answer swing? One assumption sets the range
The estimate for the baseline need for units is only as firm as its household-size assumption. Holding the county’s actual 2.78-person household size average constant yields about 269 units needed per year, whereas letting size drift down to 2.60 people per household pushes the baseline units needed to 361 units. Therefore, a plausible reading of the same population projection spans roughly 269–361 units per year.








Figure 7.4: Household-size assumptions put annual need between 270 and 360 units





269 units per year is a conservative floor of that estimate range, not its midpoint, sitting essentially on the 2020–2025 permit pace of 266 units/yr.2
2 The Greater Piedmont study’s 307 units/yr estimate falls inside the range, back-implying about a 2.7-person household.The floor is the locally-grounded case: Fauquier’s own household size has not fallen, measuring about 2.76 in 2010 and 2.76 in 2020 (decennial), and 2.78 in 2024 (ACS). This household size is flat-to-rising, bucking the national downward drift. The 361/yr high end of this estimate range, therefore, is not an extrapolation of local history. It is a sensitivity that assumes the county begins converging toward the smaller households as otherwise seen statewide (Virginia averages 2.52).

title: 7  Projected Housing Needs
section: 7.5 From new arrivals to full need: a scope ladder
text:
7.5 From new arrivals to full need: a scope ladder
How widely “need” is defined changes the units needed. Policy is what can ensure housing unit types developed meet the needs of Fauquier’s new arrivals. Read strictly, the county needs 6,795 units to house projected household growth or about 261/yr. Adding a 3% vacancy allowance lifts that to 6,999 or 269/yr until 2050.
Layering in today’s affordability backlog adds roughly 3,596 units that are needed. This is calculated with a data-grounded 1,059-unit rental deficit estimated for below 80% AMI households (Figure 5.4), plus a conservative, assumption-driven estimate for 2,537 ownership units. The estimated ownership share needed is about one-third of the 7,612 units estimated for the sub-80%-AMI ownership shortfall (the raw for-sale snapshot is not a build target). Adding in these estimates raises the need to 10,595 units built or 408/yr.








Figure 7.5: The ‘units needed’ total depends on how widely you define need











WarningReading the ladder



The two rightmost rungs are determined partly on stated assumptions and should be read as scope, not precision.


The county’s stock is aging — median year built 1987, with about 56% built before 1990, so some replacement demand is real even though its size is assumed. To replace obsolete stock involves an assumption since permits capture additions, but not demolitions. At a conservative 0.25%/yr of the 28,621-unit stock, adds about 1,860 units in replaced/updated housing stock.
Altogether, the full-scope total comes near 12,455 units or 479/yr to add supply, add additional under 80% AMI units, and replace low quality/ high maintenance stock.
The single “units needed” number is a definitional choice, not a fact. Housing only new arrivals points to needing about 269/yr. Also clearing the existing shortfall for lower income households - the vast majority of the county - and replacing obsolete stock roughly doubles that. 
Critically, the headline ~7,000-unit need already approaches — and the full-scope 12,455 far exceeds — the county’s existing by-right service-district build-out capacity; see Chapter 8 for the policy implications.

title: 7  Projected Housing Needs
text:
7.6 An aging county: the 65+ surge
The 65-and-older population climbs from 17,157 in 2030 to 18,246 in 2040, then holds essentially flat at 18,208 in 2050, as the leading edge of the baby-boom cohort ages through. The surge is concentrated in the next 15 years.








Figure 7.6: Residents 75 and older grow by a third through 2040 before leveling off





The 75-and-older group grows faster and deeper, from 7,371 to 9,939 before easing to 9,844. The higher-need and older-senior share of all seniors rises from about 43% to 54% over the next 20 years. This is the forward-looking counterpart to the current-state senior profile in Chapter 6 (65+ already 17% of residents, most owning their homes). The demand signal is for accessible, lower-maintenance, and smaller units, where aging-in-place options and downsizing product in the current stock largely lacks.

The single largest block is owner households above 100% AMI or 3,566 units - who are likely already served by current permitting and development plans.

In the lowest owner and renter income bands, the current affordable-unit deficit (from Chapter 5) dwarfs the projected new need.
