Interviewees put the problem plainly: “Aging in place and downsizing seniors and returning young people have no options.”


The county must add about 269 units per year to keep pace with household formation. By addressing seniors’ needs, with accessible and low maintenance housing options, young folks returning will be competing for the same units. Without addressing this gap in options across the household spectrum, the supply in the county will continue to increase but only widens the housing and affordability gap.






NoteWhat we heard



Interviewees recognized that limited supply and developable land shift the tax share onto remaining homeowners and businesses. That narrowed tax base strains school maintenance, infrastructure upkeep, and the remaining service districts where housing development is actually permitted. They described county infrastructure as already under pressure and almost at capacity, yet deeply needed to expand housing and business opportunities. Some stakeholders asked whether the aggressive pace of conservation has outrun its course, and wanted to allow some modest, moderated growth.








TipTown spotlight — Warrenton grows with the county; Bealeton is folded into the county total



Weldon Cooper projects the Town of Warrenton to grow from 10,693 residents in 2030 to 12,841 by 2050 (+2,148, 20.1%), a pace close to the county’s own 20.1% over 2030–2050 (Figure 7.1). As a major water-and-sewer service area within the county’s eight service districts, Warrenton is where much of the projected household growth can physically be absorbed. Bealeton is not projected separately — Weldon Cooper publishes totals only for counties and large incorporated towns, and Bealeton is an unincorporated census-designated place — so its share of growth is carried inside the Fauquier County totals throughout this chapter.

title: 8  Conclusions
text:
8.1 Projected need outpaces by-right service-district capacity
Fauquier is growing, and accommodating the most vulnerable Fauquier residents means increasing estimated unit counts that cover more than just net in-migration. This is especially important to consider with an aging population, paired with aging infrastructure, as across both renter and owner households, those making less than 80% of AMI are likely cost-burdened. With less income, that cost-burden only increases across the board throughout the county - leaving those who work here unable to afford to live here.
The average local wage narrowly covers the median rent, but wages in health care, local government, and retail fall below it, and no wage level reaches the cost of a median-priced home. Median rent is about $1,613 a month throughout the county, in homes that are mostly single family. However, vacancies for rentals priced below $1,700 a month are few and far between. Only 14% of rentals are priced under $1,000, adding to scarcity for the lowest income residents. The county’s homeownership market is also mostly available to higher earning households, where “starter homes” and units to age in place are scarce. Units priced under $350,000 represent only about 6% of 2025 sales. Overall, 21% of Fauquier’s households rent with a concentration of renters in Warrenton, where 37% of the town’s households are renters.
Who lives in Fauquier and who works in Fauquier is a completely different answer, as well. The majority of working households commute away from the county, with 37% of those working households commuting for 45 minutes or more a day. As such, in-county jobs pay modestly and most workers commute in, but live full time elsewhere. Vacancy remains low throughout the county, though it has loosened since the pandemic: apartment vacancy reached about 4.0% in 2026 Q3, and for-sale supply has averaged about 4.5 months in 2026, still short of a balanced market.
Missing middle housing, structures with two to four units, is virtually nonexistent in the study area. Presumably, gentle increases in density could house working households within the county, however, most permits approved in the county are for single family sale properties, including all 417 units permitted in 2025 and all 252 so far in 2026 - emphasizing a market focus on upper income commuters that can afford the bigger builds compared with smaller resales.
Gaps such as these are identified throughout the study and offer opportunities for increased awareness of the mismatches between need and availability. Addressing gaps and barriers to housing in Fauquier will likely involve collaborative interventions that cross sectors.
The projections chapter’s scope ladder (Figure 7.5) shows the county needs between roughly 7,000 units (housing projected household growth plus a vacancy allowance) and 12,455 units (adding today’s affordability backlog and replacement of aging stock) through 2050.
These figures should be read against a hard physical constraint documented in Chapter 1: the county’s Comprehensive Plan designates eight service districts where public water and sewer — and therefore virtually all new residential development — are permitted. The total by-right build-out capacity within those districts is approximately 8,381 units, based on the Comprehensive Plan’s own accounting.
That 8,381 figure is a 2010 baseline. The county has permitted about 4,320 units since 2010 (roughly 260 a year, through September 2026), which would leave about 4,100 if all of them fell inside the service districts. Allowing for permits outside the districts, remaining by-right capacity today is plausibly nearer 4,000–4,500 units, well below even the headline 7,000-unit need, and far below the full-scope 12,455.
Therefore, meeting the county’s projected housing need under current zoning and service-district boundaries is not physically possible. Closing any meaningful share of the need requires one or more of the following:
This is not an argument for any particular policy choice — the tradeoffs among growth, infrastructure, rural character, and affordability are for the community and its elected officials to weigh. It is an argument that the choice cannot be deferred: the gap between projected need and current build-out capacity means every decade of inaction narrows the options further. The 8,381 figure in the Comprehensive Plan was already a 2010 snapshot; updated to reflect post-2010 permitting, the remaining headroom is smaller still.

text:
A.2 Affordability calculations
Maximum affordable rent is 30% of gross monthly income. Maximum affordable purchase price is the loan a household can carry at a 28% front-end ratio, after a fixed monthly allowance for taxes and insurance, divided by one minus the down payment (a 10% down payment means the loan covers 90% of the price). The mortgage rate is the latest monthly PMMS 30-year average. The same assumptions produce the income needed to buy the median home (Chapter 5). An earlier version of this calculation multiplied the loan by 0.9 instead of dividing by it, which understated affordable prices by about a fifth; it was corrected in October 2026.

title: Appendix A — Data notes
text:
A.3 Town-level home prices
Town prices in the ownership chapter come from Bright MLS’s published town-area statistics for Warrenton and Bealeton. Annual figures are sales-weighted averages of monthly medians. The ZIP codes that carry the town names (20186/20187 and 22712) cover large rural areas outside the towns and run higher; they are noted for context only.

title: Appendix A — Data notes
text:
A.4 CoStar rent types
CoStar classifies each property’s rent type. Properties marked Affordable or Market/Affordable (rent-restricted, subsidized or mixed-income) are grouped as affordable; the rest are market-rate. Most of the units CoStar tracks with quarterly rents are at affordable properties. Rents in the rental chapter are shown in current dollars; inflation comparisons use CPI-U less shelter.

title: Appendix A — Data notes
text:
A.5 Population series
Two population estimates appear in this report, a year apart. The demographics chapter (Chapter 2) leads with the U.S. Census Bureau Population Estimates Program (PEP) July 1, 2025 estimate (Vintage 2025) — 76,503 — because PEP is the current, point-in-time measure best suited to describing recent growth.
The projections chapter (Chapter 7) bases its household-formation and forward-need estimates on the ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimate — 74,577 (Table B01003) — because the projections model is built on ACS-derived household size (2.78, B25010) and CHAS affordability shares, which are themselves 5-year-pooled measures. Using the same ACS universe keeps the inputs internally consistent. These are different measures of the same underlying population (PEP is a point-in-time July estimate; ACS 5-year is a period estimate pooling surveys from roughly 2022 in concept), so the ~1,900-person gap (about 1,300 against the PEP 2024 estimate; PEP is a year ahead of the ACS period) is expected. Readers comparing the two chapters should not assume one figure is wrong.

title: Appendix A — Data notes
section: A.6 ACS estimates labeled by a single year
text:
A.6 ACS estimates labeled by a single year
All figures and tables in this report that cite a single calendar year for American Community Survey data (e.g., “2024”) are drawn from ACS 5-year estimates referenced by their end year. The “2024” estimates pool survey responses collected from 2020 through 2024.
Five-year estimates are used throughout because Fauquier County and especially its two places (Warrenton, Bealeton) have populations too small for reliable 1-year ACS estimates. Readers should not interpret a “2024” ACS figure as a point-in-time 2024 value; it reflects conditions across the full five-year survey window, with the center of the period near 2022.

section: A.7 Bright MLS and CoStar vintages
text:
A.7 Bright MLS and CoStar vintages
Bright MLS transaction exports run through 10/30/2026. Annual sales counts for 2016–2021 come from the Greater Piedmont REALTOR / VAR series; 2022 onward come from the Bright MLS closed-sales exports. 2026 is a partial year (821 closings through October); any 2026 comparison is made against the same months of 2025.
Two active-listing snapshots are drawn from the same 10/30/2026 export and kept separate: 267 active for-sale listings (used for the listing counts in the ownership and affordability-gap chapters) and 41 active rental listings (used only for the asking-rent comparison in the rental chapter). Rental listings are a small, single-day snapshot; read them as directional.
Monthly summary series (published Bright MLS summaries, Fauquier, Warrenton, Bealeton) run January 2022 through October 2026. The final month is partial and is labeled as such where it is quoted.
Published vs. transaction-derived counts. The published monthly summary reports roughly 17–23% more sales than the transaction-level exports (a property-type filter in the exports). Median sale prices agree to about 0.1%. Sales volume is charted from the transaction export and the monthly summary is used for supply and days-on-market; neither source is re-based on the other, and the active-listing snapshot carries the same narrower definition as the export.
CoStar multifamily quarterly data run 2016 Q1 through 2026 Q3, covering 14 tracked apartment properties (about 998 units) within a broader inventory of 41 multifamily properties. CoStar covers professionally managed apartments only and is supplemental to the ACS rent anchor used for affordability.
